doc.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023

title: Times, dignity and race
summary: Whether the era shaped Coltrane; the dignity of Cranshaw, Wess and Clark Terry; a museum visit in Jackson, Mississippi, and Claude Gordon's advice.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Is there something about the times and the state of society that you think might make what you’re describing very hard to ever reproduce? And the reason I ask that is I spoke to Rashied Ali once and was trying to get at the attitude of the musicians when he played in late Coltrane’s life. And he just kept saying, “Listen, the times were different. The bebop people had their time, this was our time.” So I’m not asking this question very well but do you think that the time and space that John Coltrane was doing that in contributed to what he produced?

Well I’m sure it did and especially, you know I think about this because I was very lucky to get to play a lot with Bob Cranshaw for instance and with Frank Wess and with Joe, and those musicians, Clark Terry, those guys, they treated everybody with such dignity and respect. And you know that they weren’t treated with dignity and respect, but they were so elegant and so — they were big people, big humans. A couple of days ago we were in Jackson, Mississippi and Dorian Hall, this singer, who is a black cat on James’s band and I were in the museum together and there was a video presentation, it was a white artist, I don’t remember his name, but there was a screen with four panels. And there was a violinist, a white violinist, a white cellist, a white bassist, female bassist, and a black cat, bearded, two gold teeth, the kind of hat that the reggae guys wear, and he was singing what was a traditional song called “The Slaves’ Lament.” And the arrangement was beautiful man, a beautiful arrangement for strings. So the contrast of these white musicians playing and him singing — and you know at the same time that it was beautiful I had this feeling like we are so fucked up and you know it’s like — is it ever © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
going to change. Like sometimes I think the original sin is so great that you know what I mean? I’m an optimistic person but there are times when it’s like wow.
Yeah. We can’t outlive that or how is it solvable? That legacy.
Yeah. Well, like Claude Gordon used to say, “Straight ahead and strive for tone.”
